sentences.text: Aussiedraco is a genus of pterosaur, a type of flying reptile that lived during the Early Cretaceous period.
This extinct basal ornithocheiroid pterodactyloid pterosaur is known from a single fragment of a lower jawbone called a dentary.
The holotype fragment of the mandibular symphysis, which is the specimen the species is based on, measures about 88 mm in length.
Aussiedraco is distinguished from all other pterosaurs by having a convex top mandibular margin and a straight bottom margin.
It possesses two folds on the tip of its lower jaw, a feature not found in other pterosaurs.
Based on empty elliptical tooth sockets, the lower jaw likely carried at least five pairs of teeth.
Isolated postcranial remains including shoulder girdles, vertebrae, and wing parts have been found in the Toolebuc Formation, though their assignment to Aussiedraco remains unconfirmed.
The two folds on the lower jaw tip of Aussiedraco are unique among pterosaurs but might be an artifact of fossil preparation or a split groove.

Before 1980, no pterosaur material had been reported from Australia in scientific literature, but Aussiedraco fossils were unearthed in the 1970s from the Toolebuc Formation in western Queensland, Australia.
The fossil of Aussiedraco was first discovered in the 1970s in western Queensland.
Aussiedraco was initially described in 1980 by Ralph E. Molnar and Richard A. Thulborn as belonging to the genus Ornithocheirus.
Before being recognized as a new genus, the Aussiedraco fossil was assigned to Ornithocheirus, Anhanguera, and Lonchodectes.
Aussiedraco was named by Alexander W.A. Kellner, Taissa Rodrigues, and Fabiana R. Costa in 2011.
The anatomy of Aussiedraco's tooth sockets suggests its bottom and top teeth could interlock, particularly at the front margin.
The first four tooth sockets are positioned vertically and forward, causing the teeth to project outward.
The frontmost two pairs of tooth sockets in Aussiedraco are longer than those in Ferrodraco, indicating larger front teeth.
A 2006 study by André J. Veldmeijer and colleagues suggested ornithocheiromorphs like Aussiedraco likely had fish-eating diets based on aquatic habitats, interlocking teeth, and forward-facing eyes.
Researchers hypothesized that ornithocheiromorphs hunted small fish or swallowed them after pre-digestion because their teeth lacked chewing adaptations.
In 2012, Mark Witton suggested that the protruding sharp teeth at the front of ornithocheiromorph jaws were specialized for catching prey from water without landing.
In 2011, Kellner, Rodrigues, and Costa identified QM F10613 as a new species, Aussiedraco molnari.
Kellner and colleagues assigned Aussiedraco to the clade Pteranodontoidea.
Kellner and colleagues stated that Aussiedraco is closely allied with Anhangueridae but is not a member of it.
The genus authority for Aussiedraco is Kellner, Rodrigues & Costa, 2011.
Kellner and colleagues assigned Aussiedraco to the clade Pteranodontoidea, which contains essentially the same species as Ornithocheiroidea.
Aussiedraco lived during the Early Cretaceous period in what is now Australia.
Aussiedraco lived between 106.3 and 100.5 million years ago during the Albian stage.
During the Albian stage, the Toolebuc Formation where Aussiedraco lived was a near-shore open ocean with low oxygenated waters.
The Toolebuc Formation was deposited at the southern edge of the Toolebuc Sea, which had deep anaerobic waters to the north and shallow aerobic brackish waters to the south.
Aussiedraco lived alongside the pterosaurs Mythunga, Ferrodraco, and Haliskia in the Toolebuc Formation.
It is currently impossible to confirm if isolated postcranial remains from the Toolebuc Formation belong to Aussiedraco due to a lack of overlapping material.
While the unique jaw folds of Aussiedraco resemble those of Cearadactylus, suggesting they might be the same taxon, this is unlikely given the lack of confirmation and their different origins.
The ecology and diet of Aussiedraco and similar ornithocheiromorphs remain debated topics among scientists.
